prompt: Write a rule set that turns LaTeX arithmetic into words a screen reader can speak: a-b becomes "a minus b", a\cdot b becomes "a times b", a\div b becomes "a divided by b", and anything else passes through unchanged. Test it on 7-2, 3\cdot 4 and 9\div 3.

Normalize inequalities so there is exactly one space on each side of the operator for \le, \ge, 
e and 
less. Tests: x\le3 should give x \le 3, y\ge-1 should give y \ge -1, a
e b should give a 
e b, and 2
less1 should give 2 
less 1.

I need a words table that rewrites Greek letter commands to plain ASCII names for a search index: \theta to theta, \nu to nu, \tau to tau, \rho to rho and \omega to omega. Keep a pass-through catch-all rule and add one test per letter.

Translate LaTeX into calculator syntax: \frac{a}{b} becomes (a)/(b), a^{b} becomes a^(b), \sqrt{x} becomes sqrt(x), and a\times b becomes a*b. Include tests for \frac{1}{2}, x^{3}, \sqrt{16} and 4\times5.

Subtracting or multiplying by a negative number should put the negative in parentheses: 5-{-3} becomes 5-\left(-3\right) and 2*{-4} becomes 2\times\left(-4\right), while plain 5-3 stays 5-3 and 2*4 becomes 2\times 4. Write the rules and a test for each of those four inputs.

Inside the subscript of a summation, rewrite = as \coloneqq, so \sum_{i=1}^{n} i becomes \sum_{i \coloneqq 1}^{n}{i}. Outside a sum, = must be left as an ordinary equals sign with spaces, so x=1 becomes x = 1. Test both.

Define a type called signedNumber that matches a number or a minus sign followed by a number, then use it in a rule so two juxtaposed signed numbers like {-2}{3} are written as (-2)(3). Add a catch-all and test {-2}{3} and {4}{-5}.
Our item bank writes large numbers with comma thousands separators. Make a rule set that allows thousands separators and passes numbers and addition through, with tests for 1,250,000 and 12,500+3.
Configure the rule set for European number formatting: comma as the decimal separator and period as the thousands separator. Pass expressions through unchanged, and test 3,14 and 1.000,5+2.
Turn on interval parsing so half-open and closed intervals survive translation. Rules should reproduce \left(?\right], \left[?\right) and \left[?\right] as written. Test (0,1], [2,5) and [-1,1].
Answers sometimes include units like 5\text{ cm}+3\text{ cm}. Set the option that ignores \text so the units drop out, keep addition as %1+%2, and test that input plus 12\text{ kg}.
A rule set where a coefficient of one is ignored, so 1x+2 is treated like x+2. Rules for addition and juxtaposition plus a catch-all; tests for 1x+2 and 1y.

Write rules for square roots and nth roots that keep them in LaTeX form. I don't know the exact expected output yet, so add tests for \sqrt{2}, \sqrt[3]{8} and \sqrt{x+1} that just capture what the rule set produces today.
Wrap the operand of postfix operators in braces: n! becomes {n}!, 40% becomes {40}%, and 90\degree becomes {90}\degree. Add a test for each.
Speak set notation: A\cup B reads "A union B", A\cap B reads "A intersect B", and A\backslash B reads "A minus B". Tests for all three.

Translate a bmatrix into a nested list: each row becomes [a, b] and the whole matrix becomes [[...], [...]], using %* to repeat over rows and over the entries within a row. Test \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}.

Definite and indefinite integrals should come out with braces on the bounds and a space before the differential: \int_0^1 x dx becomes \int_{0}^{1} x dx and \int x^2 dx becomes \int {x}^{2} dx. Put the definite rule before the indefinite one and test both.
Words table: map \leq to \le and \geq to \ge so both spellings normalize. Rules: ?\le? to %1\le %2, ?\ge? to %1\ge %2, and a catch-all. Tests: a\leq b and c\geq d.
Add division with \div, spaced like the other operators, and add a test for 8\div2.
The two tests have empty expectations. Fill them in with what each one should produce under these rules, and add a test for x^{2}+1.
